Before the inheritance by the New Testament (for here the idea of the "INHERITANCE," following as the result of Christ's "death," being introduced, requires the Greek to be translated "testament," as it was before covenant) could come in, there must be redemption of (that is, deliverance from the penalties incurred by) the transgressions committed under the first testament, for the propitiatory sacrifices under the first testament reached only as far as removing outward ceremonial defilement. But in order to obtain the inheritance which is a reality, there must be a real propitiation, since God could not enter into covenant relation with us so long as past sins were unexpiated; <reference osisRef="Rom.3.24">Ro 3:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.25">25</reference>, "a propitiation ... His righteousness for the remission of sins that are past."<div eID="gen38809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38810" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">might--</hi>Greek, "may receive," which previously they could not (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.39">He 11:39</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.40">40</reference>).<div eID="gen38810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38811" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the promise--</hi>to Abraham. <div eID="gen38811" type="x-p"/>
entries.62901414280c6cdb68d1b2b3c91f74e039bfb78c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18476"/><div sID="gen38812" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18476"/>16. A general axiomatic truth; it is "a testament"; not the testament. The testator must die before his testament takes effect (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.17">He 9:17</reference>). This is a common meaning of the Greek noun diathece. So in <reference osisRef="Luke.22.29">Lu 22:29</reference>, "I appoint (by testamentary disposition; the cognate Greek verb diatithemai) unto you a kingdom, as my Father hath appointed unto me." The need of death before the testamentary appointment takes effect, holds good in Christ's relation as MAN to us; Of course not in God's relation to Christ.<div eID="gen38812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38813" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be--</hi>literally, be borne": "be involved in the case"; be inferred; or else, "be brought forward in court," so as to give effect to the will. This sense (testament) of the Greek "diathece" here does not exclude its other secondary senses in the other passages of the New Testament: (1) a covenant between two parties; (2) an arrangement, or disposition, made by God alone in relation to us. Thus, <reference osisRef="Matt.26.28">Mt 26:28</reference> may be translated, "Blood of the covenant"; for a testament does not require blood shedding. Compare <reference osisRef="Exod.24.8">Ex 24:8</reference> (covenant), which Christ quotes, though it is probable He included in a sense "testament" also under the Greek word diathece (comprehending both meanings, "covenant" and "testament"), as this designation strictly and properly applies to the new dispensation, and is rightly applicable to the old also, not in itself, but when viewed as typifying the new, which is properly a testament. Moses (<reference osisRef="Exod.24.8">Ex 24:8</reference>) speaks of the same thing as [Christ and] Paul. Moses, by the term "covenant," does not mean aught save one concerning giving the heavenly inheritance typified by Canaan after the death of the Testator, which he represented by the sprinkling of blood. And Paul, by the term "testament," does not mean aught save one having conditions attached to it, one which is at the same time a covenant [Poli, Synopsis]; the conditions are fulfilled by Christ, not by us, except that we must believe, but even this God works in His people. Tholuck explains, as elsewhere, "covenant ... covenant ... mediating victim"; the masculine is used of the victim personified, and regarded as mediator of the covenant; especially as in the new covenant a MAN (Christ) took the place of the victim. The covenanting parties used to pass between the divided parts of the sacrificed animals; but, without reference to this rite, the need of a sacrifice for establishing a covenant sufficiently explains this verse. Others, also, explaining the Greek as "covenant," consider that the death of the sacrificial victim represented in all covenants the death of both parties as unalterably bound to the covenant. So in the redemption-covenant, the death of Jesus symbolized the death of God (?) in the person of the mediating victim, and the death of man in the same. But the expression is not "there must be the death of both parties making the covenant," but singular, "of Him who made (aorist, past time; not 'of Him making') the testament." Also, it is "death," not "sacrifice" or "slaying." Plainly, the death is supposed to be past (aorist, "made"); and the fact of the death is brought (Greek) before court to give effect to the will. These requisites of a will, or testament, concur here: (1) a testator; (2) heirs; (3) goods; (4) the death of the testator; (5) the fact of the death brought forward in court. In <reference osisRef="Matt.26.28">Mt 26:28</reference> two other requisites appear: witnesses, the disciples; and a seal, the sacrament of the Lord's Supper, the sign of His blood wherewith the testament is primarily sealed. It is true the heir is ordinarily the successor of him who dies and so ceases to have the possession. But in this case Christ comes to life again, and is Himself (including all that He hath), in the power of His now endless life, His people's inheritance; in His being Heir (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.2">He 1:2</reference>), they are heirs. <div eID="gen38813" type="x-p"/>
entries.5609438a91ba360eea90950188d59c357237e9bc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18477"/><div sID="gen38814" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18477"/><hi type="bold">17. after--</hi>literally, "over," as we say "upon the death of the testators"; not as Tholuck, "on the condition that slain sacrifices be there," which the Greek hardly sanctions.<div eID="gen38814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38815" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">otherwise--</hi>"seeing that it is never availing" [Alford]. Bengel and Lachmann read with an interrogation, "Since, is it ever in force (surely not) while the testator liveth?" <div eID="gen38815" type="x-p"/>
entries.8d0f554adb6fc90052b90f0de8d42a20cd03b441: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18478"/><div sID="gen38816" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18478"/><hi type="bold">18. Whereupon--</hi>rather, "Whence."<div eID="gen38816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38817" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dedicated--</hi>"inaugurated." The Old Testament strictly and formally began on that day of inauguration. "Where the disposition, or arrangement, is ratified by the blood of another, namely, of animals, which cannot make a covenant, much less make a testament, it is not strictly a testament, where it is ratified by the death of him that makes the arrangement, it is strictly, Greek 'diathece,' Hebrew 'berith,' taken in a wider sense, a testament" [Bengel]; thus, in <reference osisRef="Heb.9.18">He 9:18</reference>, referring to the old dispensation, we may translate, "the first (covenant)": or better, retain "the first (testament)," not that the old dispensation, regarded by itself, is a testament, but it is so when regarded as the typical representative of the new, which is strictly a Testament. <div eID="gen38817" type="x-p"/>
entries.415a03e75bffd579f0e5b0ecbf00dd2da99aadd3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18479"/><div sID="gen38818" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18479"/><hi type="bold">19. For--</hi>confirming the general truth, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.16">He 9:16</reference>.<div eID="gen38818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38819" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">spoken ... according to the law--</hi>strictly adhering to every direction of "the law of commandments contained in ordinances" (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.15">Ep 2:15</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Exod.24.3">Ex 24:3</reference>, "Moses told the people all the words of the Lord, and all the judgments; and all the people answered with one voice," &c.<div eID="gen38819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38820" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the blood of calves--</hi>Greek, "the calves," namely, those sacrificed by the "young men" whom he sent to do so (<reference osisRef="Exod.24.5">Ex 24:5</reference>). The "peace offerings" there mentioned were "of oxen" (Septuagint, "little calves"), and the "burnt offerings" were probably (though this is not specified), as on the day of atonement, goats. The law in Exodus sanctioned formally many sacrificial practices in use by tradition, from the primitive revelation long before.<div eID="gen38820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38821" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with water--</hi>prescribed, though not in the twenty-fourth chapter of Exodus, yet in other purifications; for example, of the leper, and the water of separation which contained the ashes of the red heifer.<div eID="gen38821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38822" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">scarlet wool, and hyssop--</hi>ordinarily used for purification. Scarlet or crimson, resembling blood: it was thought to be a peculiarly deep, fast dye, whence it typified sin (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.1.18">Is 1:18</reference>). So Jesus wore a scarlet robe, the emblem of the deep-dyed sins He bore on Him, though He had none in Him. Wool was used as imbibing and retaining water; the hyssop, as a bushy, tufty plant (wrapt round with the scarlet wool), was used for sprinkling it. The wool was also a symbol of purity (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.18">Is 1:18</reference>). The Hyssopus officinalis grows on walls, with small lancet-formed woolly leaves, an inch long, with blue and white flowers, and a knotty stalk about a foot high.<div eID="gen38822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38823" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sprinkled ... the book--</hi>namely, out of which he had read "every precept": the book of the testament or covenant. This sprinkling of the book is not mentioned in the twenty-fourth chapter of Exodus. Hence Bengel translates, "And (having taken) the book itself (so <reference osisRef="Exod.24.7">Ex 24:7</reference>), he both sprinkled all the people, and (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.21">He 9:21</reference>) moreover sprinkled the tabernacle." But the Greek supports English Version. Paul, by inspiration, supplies the particular specified here, not in <reference osisRef="Exod.24.7">Ex 24:7</reference>. The sprinkling of the roll (so the Greek for "book") of the covenant, or testament, as well as of the people, implies that neither can the law be fulfilled, nor the people be purged from their sins, save by the sprinkling of the blood of Christ (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.2">1Pe 1:2</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Heb.9.23">He 9:23</reference>, which shows that there is something antitypical to the Bible in heaven itself (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.20.12">Re 20:12</reference>). The Greek, "itself," distinguishes the book itself from the "precepts" in it which he "spake." <div eID="gen38823" type="x-p"/>
entries.ad13defb45bb008cb9f2179239a31a1074432977: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18480"/><div sID="gen38824" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18480"/>20. <reference osisRef="Exod.24.8">Ex 24:8</reference>, "Behold the blood of the covenant, which the Lord has made with you concerning all these words." The change is here made to accord with Christ's inauguration of the new testament, or covenant, as recorded in <reference osisRef="Luke.22.20">Lu 22:20</reference>, "This cup (is) the new Testament in My blood, which is shed for you": the only Gospel in which the "is" has to be supplied. Luke was Paul's companion, which accounts for the correspondence, as here too "is" has to be supplied.<div eID="gen38824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38825" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">testament--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Heb.9.16">He 9:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.17">17</reference>). The Greek "diathece" means both "testament" and "covenant": the term "covenant" better suits the old dispensation, though the idea testament is included, for the old was one in its typical relation to the new dispensation, to which the term "testament" is better suited. Christ has sealed the testament with His blood, of which the Lord's Supper is the sacramental sign. The testator was represented by the animals slain in the old dispensation. In both dispensations the inheritance was bequeathed: in the new by One who has come in person and died; in the old by the same one, only typically and ceremonially present. See Alford's excellent Note.<div eID="gen38825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38826" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">enjoined unto you--</hi>commissioned me to ratify in relation to you. In the old dispensation the condition to be fulfilled on the people's part is implied in the words, <reference osisRef="Exod.24.8">Ex 24:8</reference>, "(Lord made with you) concerning all these words." But here Paul omits this clause, as he includes the fulfilment of this condition of obedience to "all these words" in the new covenant, as part of God's promise, in <reference osisRef="Heb.8.8">He 8:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.12">10, 12</reference>, whereby Christ fulfils all for our justification, and will enable us by putting His Spirit in us to fulfil all in our now progressive, and finally complete, sanctification. <div eID="gen38826" type="x-p"/>
entries.55aad2f564e2ac0b27bcc1db88ecc8150fe5c330: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18481"/><div sID="gen38827" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18481"/>21. Greek, "And, moreover, in like manner." The sprinkling of the tabernacle with blood is added by inspiration here to the account in Ex 30:25-30; 40:<reference osisRef="Exod.9.10">9, 10</reference>, which mentions only Moses' anointing the tabernacle and its vessels. In <reference osisRef="Lev.8.10">Le 8:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.15.30">15, 30</reference>, the sprinkling of blood upon Aaron and his garments, and upon his sons, and upon the altar, is mentioned as well as the anointing, so that we might naturally infer, as Josephus has distinctly stated, that the tabernacle and its vessels were sprinkled with blood as well as being anointed: <reference osisRef="Lev.16.16">Le 16:16</reference>, 20, 33, virtually sanctions this inference. The tabernacle and its contents needed purification (<reference osisRef="2Chr.29.21">2Ch 29:21</reference>). <div eID="gen38827" type="x-p"/>
entries.f234ac966445935f47619ee7b4f920250dfc940f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18482"/><div sID="gen38828" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18482"/><hi type="bold">22. almost--</hi>to be joined with "all things," namely almost all things under the old dispensation. The exceptions to all things being purified by blood are, <reference osisRef="Exod.19.10">Ex 19:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.15.5">Le 15:5</reference>, &c.; 16:26, 28; 22:6; <reference osisRef="Num.31.22-Num.31.24">Nu 31:22-24</reference>.<div eID="gen38828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38829" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">without--</hi>Greek, "apart from."<div eID="gen38829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38830" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shedding of blood--</hi>shed in the slaughter of the victim, and poured out at the altar subsequently. The pouring out of the blood on the altar is the main part of the sacrifice (<reference osisRef="Lev.17.11">Le 17:11</reference>), and it could not have place apart from the previous shedding of the blood in the slaying. Paul has, perhaps, in mind here, <reference osisRef="Luke.22.20">Lu 22:20</reference>, "This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you."<div eID="gen38830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38831" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is--</hi>Greek, "takes place": comes to pass.<div eID="gen38831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38832" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">remission--</hi>of sins: a favorite expression of Luke, Paul's companion. Properly used of remitting a debt (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.12">Mt 6:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.18.27">18:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.18.32">32</reference>); our sins are debts. On the truth here, compare <reference osisRef="Lev.5.11-Lev.5.13">Le 5:11-13</reference>, an exception because of poverty, confirming the general rule. <div eID="gen38832" type="x-p"/>
entries.843fca3241c101d038807106d3d26cbd41433f68: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18483"/><div sID="gen38833" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18483"/><hi type="bold">23. patterns--</hi>"the suggestive representations"; the typical copies (see on <reference osisRef="Heb.8.5">He 8:5</reference>).<div eID="gen38833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38834" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">things in the heavens--</hi>the heavenly tabernacle and the things therein.<div eID="gen38834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38835" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">purified with these--</hi>with the blood of bulls and goats.<div eID="gen38835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38836" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heavenly things themselves--</hi>the archetypes. Man's sin had introduced an element of disorder into the relations of God and His holy angels in respect to man. The purification removes this element of disorder and changes God's wrath against man in heaven (designed to be the place of God's revealing His grace to men and angels) into a smile of reconciliation. Compare "peace in heaven" (<reference osisRef="Luke.19.38">Lu 19:38</reference>). "The uncreated heaven of God, though in itself untroubled light, yet needed a purification in so far as the light of love was obscured by the fire of wrath against sinful man" [Delitzsch in Alford]. Contrast <reference osisRef="Rev.12.7-Rev.12.10">Re 12:7-10</reference>. Christ's atonement had the effect also of casting Satan out of heaven (<reference osisRef="Luke.10.18">Lu 10:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.31">Joh 12:31</reference>, compare <reference osisRef="Heb.2.14">He 2:14</reference>). Christ's body, the true tabernacle (see on <reference osisRef="Heb.8.2">He 8:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.9.11">He 9:11</reference>), as bearing our imputed sin (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.21">2Co 5:21</reference>), was consecrated (<reference osisRef="John.17.17">Joh 17:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.17.19">19</reference>) and purified by the shedding of His blood to be the meeting place of God and man.<div eID="gen38836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38837" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sacrifices--</hi>The plural is used in expressing the general proposition, though strictly referring to the one sacrifice of Christ once for all. Paul implies that His one sacrifice, by its matchless excellency, is equivalent to the Levitical many sacrifices. It, though but one, is manifold in its effects and applicability to many. <div eID="gen38837" type="x-p"/>
entries.8d5952640bb9e8f228be185a7b36485947fd2769: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18484"/><div sID="gen38838" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18484"/>24. Resumption more fully of the thought, "He entered in once into the holy place," <reference osisRef="Heb.9.12">He 9:12</reference>. He has in <reference osisRef="Heb.9.13">He 9:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.14">14</reference>, expanded the words "by his own blood," <reference osisRef="Heb.9.12">He 9:12</reference>; and in <reference osisRef="Heb.9.15-Heb.9.23">He 9:15-23</reference>, he has enlarged on "an High Priest of good things to come."<div eID="gen38838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38839" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not ... into ... holy places made with hands--</hi>as was the Holy of Holies in the earthly tabernacle (see on <reference osisRef="Heb.9.11">He 9:11</reference>).<div eID="gen38839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38840" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">figures--</hi>copies "of the true" holiest place, heaven, the original archetype (<reference osisRef="Heb.8.5">He 8:5</reference>).<div eID="gen38840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38841" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">into heaven itself--</hi>the immediate presence of the invisible God beyond all the created heavens, through which latter Jesus passed (see on <reference osisRef="Heb.4.14">He 4:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.16">1Ti 6:16</reference>).<div eID="gen38841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38842" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">now--</hi>ever since His ascension in the present economy (compare <reference osisRef="Heb.9.26">He 9:26</reference>).<div eID="gen38842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38843" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to appear--</hi>To PRESENT Himself; Greek, "to be made to appear." Mere man may have a vision through a medium, or veil, as Moses had (<reference osisRef="Exod.33.18">Ex 33:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.33.20-Exod.33.23">20-23</reference>). Christ alone beholds the Father without a veil, and is His perfect image. Through seeing Him only can we see the Father.<div eID="gen38843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38844" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the presence of God--</hi>Greek, "to the face of God." The saints shall hereafter see God's face in Christ (<reference osisRef="Rev.22.4">Re 22:4</reference>): the earnest of which is now given (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.18">2Co 3:18</reference>). Aaron, the Levitical high priest for the people, stood before the ark and only saw the cloud, the symbol of God's glory (<reference osisRef="Exod.28.30">Ex 28:30</reference>).<div eID="gen38844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38845" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for us--</hi>in our behalf as our Advocate and Intercessor (<reference osisRef="Heb.7.25">He 7:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.34">Ro 8:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.2.1">1Jo 2:1</reference>). "It is enough that Jesus should show Himself for us to the Father: the sight of Jesus satisfied God in our behalf. He brings before the face of God no offering which has exhausted itself, and, as only sufficing for a time, needs renewal; but He himself is in person, by virtue of the eternal Spirit, that is, the imperishable life of His person, now and for ever freed from death, our eternally present offering before God" [Delitzsch in Alford]. <div eID="gen38845" type="x-p"/>
entries.dd499930fb0169dd1000a4b2cf269ecce7d629a1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18485"/><div sID="gen38846" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18485"/>25. As in <reference osisRef="Heb.9.24">He 9:24</reference>, Paul said, it was not into the typical, but the true sanctuary, that Christ is entered; so now he says, that His sacrifice needs not, as the Levitical sacrifices did, to be repeated. Construe, "Nor yet did He enter for this purpose that He may offer Himself often," that is, "present Himself in the presence of God, as the high priest does (Paul uses the present tense, as the legal service was then existing), year by year, on the day of atonement, entering the Holy of Holies.<div eID="gen38846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38847" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with--</hi>literally, "in."<div eID="gen38847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38848" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blood of others--</hi>not his own, as Christ did. <div eID="gen38848" type="x-p"/>
entries.2829f2cfbbe294c5229b94660562fc4144b68e36: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18486"/><div sID="gen38849" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18486"/><hi type="bold">26. then--</hi>in that case.<div eID="gen38849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38850" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">must ... have suffered--</hi>rather as Greek, "It would have been necessary for Him often to suffer." In order to "offer" (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.25">He 9:25</reference>), or present Himself often before God in the heavenly holiest place, like the legal high priests making fresh renewals of this high priestly function. He would have had, and would have often to suffer. His oblation of Himself before God was once for all (that is, the bringing in of His blood into the heavenly Holy of Holies), and therefore the preliminary suffering was once for all.<div eID="gen38850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38851" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">since the foundation of the world--</hi>The continued sins of men, from their first creation, would entail a continual suffering on earth, and consequent oblation of His blood in the heavenly holiest place, since the foundation of the world, if the one oblation "in the fulness of time" were not sufficient. Philo [The Creation of the World, p. 637], shows that the high priest of the Hebrews offered sacrifices for the whole human race. "If there had been greater efficacy in the repetition of the oblation, Christ necessarily would not have been so long promised, but would have been sent immediately after the foundation of the world to suffer, and offer Himself at successive periods" [Grotius].<div eID="gen38851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38852" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">now--</hi>as the case is,<div eID="gen38852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38853" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">once--</hi>for all; without need of renewal. Rome's fiction of an UNBLOODY sacrifice in the mass, contradicts her assertion that the blood of Christ is present in the wine; and also confutes her assertion that the mass is propitiatory; for, if unbloody, it cannot be propitiatory; for without shedding of blood there is no remission (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.22">He 9:22</reference>). Moreover, the expression "once" for all here, and in <reference osisRef="Heb.9.28">He 9:28</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Heb.10.10">He 10:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.12">12</reference>, proves the falsity of her view that there is a continually repeated offering of Christ in the Eucharist or mass. The offering of Christ was a thing once done that it might be thought of for ever (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Heb.10.12">He 10:12</reference>).<div eID="gen38853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38854" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the end of the world--</hi>Greek, "at the consummation of the ages"; the winding up of all the previous ages from the foundation of the world; to be followed by a new age (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.1">He 1:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.2">2</reference>). The last age, beyond which no further age is to be expected before Christ's speedy second coming, which is the complement of the first coming; literally, "the ends of the ages"; <reference osisRef="Matt.28.20">Mt 28:20</reference> is literally, "the consummation of the age," or world (singular; not as here, plural, ages). Compare "the fulness of times," <reference osisRef="Eph.1.10">Ep 1:10</reference>.<div eID="gen38854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38855" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">appeared--</hi>Greek, "been manifested" on earth (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.16">1Ti 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.20">1Pe 1:20</reference>). English Version has confounded three distinct Greek verbs, by translating all alike, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.24">He 9:24</reference>, 26, 28, "appear." But, in <reference osisRef="Heb.9.24">He 9:24</reference>, it is "to present Himself," namely, before God in the heavenly sanctuary; in <reference osisRef="Heb.9.26">He 9:26</reference>, "been manifested" on earth: in <reference osisRef="Heb.9.28">He 9:28</reference>, "shall be seen" by all, and especially believers.<div eID="gen38855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38856" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">put away--</hi>abolish; doing away sin's power as well by delivering men from its guilt and penalty, so that it should be powerless to condemn men, as also from its yoke, so that they shall at last sin no more.<div eID="gen38856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38857" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sin--</hi>singular number; all the sins of men of every age are regarded as one mass laid on Christ. He hath not only droned for all actual sins, but destroyed sin itself. <reference osisRef="John.1.29">Joh 1:29</reference>, "Behold the Lamb of God that taketh away the sin (not merely the sins: singular, not plural) of the world."<div eID="gen38857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38858" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by the sacrifice of himself--</hi>Greek, "by (through) His own sacrifice"; not by "blood of others" (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.25">He 9:25</reference>). Alford loses this contrast in translating, "by His sacrifice." <div eID="gen38858" type="x-p"/>
entries.6f3e09295d237e6f978d7638febc0c1a30ced837: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18487"/><div sID="gen38859" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18487"/><hi type="bold">27. as--</hi>inasmuch as.<div eID="gen38859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38860" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">it is appointed--</hi>Greek, "it is laid up (as our appointed lot)," <reference osisRef="Col.1.5">Col 1:5</reference>. The word "appointed" (so Hebrew "seth" means) in the case of man, answers to "anointed" in the case of Jesus; therefore "the Christ," that is, the anointed, is the title here given designedly. He is the representative man; and there is a strict correspondence between the history of man and that of the Son of man. The two most solemn facts of our being are here connected with the two most gracious truths of our dispensation, our death and judgment answering in parallelism to Christ's first coming to die for us, and His second coming to consummate our salvation.<div eID="gen38860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38861" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">once--</hi>and no more.<div eID="gen38861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38862" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">after this the judgment--</hi>namely, at Christ's appearing, to which, in <reference osisRef="Heb.9.28">He 9:28</reference>, "judgment" in this verse is parallel. Not, "after this comes the heavenly glory." The intermediate state is a state of joyous, or else agonizing and fearful, expectation of "judgment"; after the judgment comes the full and final state of joy, or else woe. <div eID="gen38862" type="x-p"/>
entries.87e19f3a01eaa7960410da9fc9eff70fafaf4b6f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18488"/><div sID="gen38863" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18488"/><hi type="bold">28. Christ--</hi>Greek, "THE Christ"; the representative Man; representing all men, as the first Adam did.<div eID="gen38863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38864" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">once offered--</hi>not "often," <reference osisRef="Heb.9.25">He 9:25</reference>; just as "men," of whom He is the representative Head, are appointed by God once to die. He did not need to die again and again for each individual, or each successive generation of men, for He represents all men of every age, and therefore needed to die but once for all, so as to exhaust the penalty of death incurred by all. He was offered by the Father, His own "eternal Spirit" (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.14">He 9:14</reference>) concurring; as Abraham spared not Isaac, but offered him, the son himself unresistingly submitting to the father's will (<reference osisRef="Gen.22.1-Gen.22.24">Ge 22:1-24</reference>).<div eID="gen38864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38865" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to bear the sins--</hi>referring to <reference osisRef="Isa.53.12">Is 53:12</reference>, "He bare the sins of many," namely, on Himself; so "bear" means, <reference osisRef="Lev.24.15">Le 24:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.5.31">Nu 5:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.14.34">14:34</reference>. The Greek is literally "to bear up" (<reference osisRef="1Pet.2.24">1Pe 2:24</reference>). "Our sins were laid on Him. When, therefore, He was lifted up on the cross, He bare up our sins along with Him" [Bengel].<div eID="gen38865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38866" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">many--</hi>not opposed to all, but to few. He, the One, was offered for many; and that once for all (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.20.28">Mt 20:28</reference>).<div eID="gen38866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38867" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">look for him--</hi>with waiting expectation even unto the end (so the Greek). It is translated "wait for" in <reference osisRef="Rom.8.19">Ro 8:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.23">23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.7">1Co 1:7</reference>, which see.<div eID="gen38867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38868" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">appear--</hi>rather, as Greek, "be seen." No longer in the alien "form of a servant," but in His own proper glory.<div eID="gen38868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38869" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">without sin--</hi>apart from, separate from, sin. Not bearing the sin of many on Him as at His first coming (even then there was no sin in Him). That sin has been at His first coming once for all taken away, so as to need no repetition of His sin offering of Himself (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.26">He 9:26</reference>). At His second coming He shall have no more to do with sin.<div eID="gen38869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38870" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto salvation--</hi>to bring in completed salvation; redeeming then the body which is as yet subject to the bondage of corruption. Hence, in <reference osisRef="Phil.3.20">Php 3:20</reference> he says, "we look for THE Saviour." Note, Christ's prophetical office, as the divine Teacher, was especially exercised during His earthly ministry; His priestly is now from His first to His second coming; His kingly office shall be fully manifested at, and after, His second coming. <chapter eID="Heb.9"/>

entries.9ba6f54f1db2448139154ac41c1627133ab06015: <div eID="gen53392" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen53393" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen53394" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen53394" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen53393" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen53395" type="x-p"/> Of the first covenant, and its ordinances, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.1">Heb 9:1</reference>. The tabernacle, candlestick, table, show-bread, veil, holy of holies, censer, ark, pot of manna, Aaron's rod, tables of the covenant, cherubim of glory, and mercy seat, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.2-Heb.9.5">Heb 9:2-5</reference>. How the priests served, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.6">Heb 9:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.7">Heb 9:7</reference>. What was signified by the service, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.8-Heb.9.10">Heb 9:8-10</reference>. The superior excellency of Christ's ministry and sacrifice, and the efficacy of his blood, vv. 11-26. As men must once die and be judged, so Christ was once offered to bear the sins of many, and shall come without a sin-offering, a second time, to them that expect him, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.27">Heb 9:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.28">Heb 9:28</reference>. <div eID="gen53395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53396" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen53396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53397" type="x-p"/> The first covenant had also ordinances - Our translators have introduced the word covenant, as if διαθηκη had been, if not originally in the text, yet in the apostle's mind. Several MSS., but not of good note, as well as printed editions, with the Coptic version, have σκηνη tabernacle; but this is omitted by ABDE, several others, both the Syriac, Ethiopic, Armenian, Vulgate, some copies of the Itala, and several of the Greek fathers; it is in all probability a spurious reading, the whole context showing that covenant is that to which the apostle refers, as that was the subject in the preceding chapter, and this is a continuation of the same discourse. <div eID="gen53397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53398" type="x-p"/> Ordinances - Δικαιωματα· Rites and ceremonies. <div eID="gen53398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53399" type="x-p"/> A worldly sanctuary - Ἁγιον κοσμικον. It is supposed that the term worldly, here, is opposed to the term heavenly, <reference osisRef="Heb.8.5">Heb 8:5</reference>; and that the whole should be referred to the carnality or secular nature of the tabernacle service. But I think there is nothing plainer than that the apostle is speaking here in praise of this sublimely emblematic service, and hence he proceeds to enumerate the various things contained in the first tabernacle, which added vastly to its splendor and importance; such as the table of the show-bread, the golden candlestick, the golden censer, the ark of the covenant overlaid round about with gold, in which was the golden pot that had the manna, Aaron's rod that budded, and the two tables which God had written with his own finger: hence I am led to believe that κοσμικος is here taken in its proper, natural meaning, and signifies adorned, embellished, splendid; and hence κοσμος, the world: Tota hujus universi machina, coelum et terram complectens et quicquid utroque contineter, κοσμος dicitur, quod nihil ea est mundius, pulchrius, et ornatius. "The whole machine of this universe, comprehending the heavens and the earth, and whatsoever is contained in both, is called κοσμος, because nothing is more beautiful, more fair, and more elegant." So Pliny, Hist. Nat., l. ii. c. 5: Nam quem κοσμον Graeci nomine ornamenti appellaverunt, eum nos a perfecta absolutaque elegantia, Mundum. "That which the Greeks call κοσμος, ornament, we, (the Latins), from its perfect and absolute elegance call mundum, world." See on <reference osisRef="Gen.2.1">Gen 2:1</reference> (note). <div eID="gen53399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53400" type="x-p"/> The Jews believe that the tabernacle was an epitome of the world; and it is remarkable, when speaking of their city, that they express this sentiment by the same Greek word, in Hebrew letters, which the apostle uses here: so in Bereshith Rabba, s. 19, fol. 19: כל קוזמיקון שלו שם הוא col kozmikon (κοσμικον) shelo sham hu. "All his world is placed there." Philo says much to the same purpose. <div eID="gen53400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53401" type="x-p"/> If my exposition be not admitted, the next most likely is, that God has a worldly tabernacle as well as a heavenly one; that he as truly dwelt in the Jewish tabernacle as he did in the heaven of heavens; the one being his worldly house, the other his heavenly house.
entries.fcb01cc051fa46403547f093352f670f41ac5c43: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen53401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53402" type="x-p"/> For there was a tabernacle made; the first, wherein - The sense is here very obscure, and the construction involved: leaving out all punctuation, which is the case with all the very ancient MSS., the verse stands thus: Σκηνη γαρ κατεσκευασθη ἡ πρωτη εν ᾑ ἡ τε λυχνια, κ. τ. λ. which I suppose an indifferent person, who understood the language, would without hesitation render, For, there was the first tabernacle constructed, in which were the candlestick, etc. And this tabernacle or dwelling may be called the first dwelling place which God had among men, to distinguish it from the second dwelling place, the temple built by Solomon; for tabernacle here is to be considered in its general sense, as implying a dwelling. <div eID="gen53402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53403" type="x-p"/> To have a proper understanding of what the apostle relates here, we should endeavor to take a concise view of the tabernacle erected by Moses in the wilderness. This tabernacle was the epitome of the Jewish temple; or rather, according to this as a model was the Jewish temple built. It comprised, <div eID="gen53403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53404" type="x-p"/> 1. The court where the people might enter. <div eID="gen53404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53405" type="x-p"/> 2. In this was contained the altar of burnt-offerings, on which were offered the sacrifices in general, besides offerings of bread, wine, and other things. <div eID="gen53405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53406" type="x-p"/> 3. At the bottom or lower end of this court was the tent of the covenant; the two principal parts of the tabernacle were, the holy place and the holy of holies. <div eID="gen53406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53407" type="x-p"/> In the temple built by Solomon there was a court for the Levites, different from that of the people; and, at the entrance of the holy place, a vestibule. But in the tabernacle built by Moses these parts were not found, nor does the apostle mention them here. <div eID="gen53407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53408" type="x-p"/> In the holy place, as the apostle observes, there were, <div eID="gen53408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53409" type="x-p"/> 1. The golden candlestick of seven branches, on the south. <div eID="gen53409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53410" type="x-p"/> 2. The golden altar, or altar of incense, on the north. <div eID="gen53410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53411" type="x-p"/> 3. The altar, or table of the show-bread; or where the twelve loaves, representing the twelve tribes, were laid before the Lord. <div eID="gen53411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53412" type="x-p"/> 1. In each branch of the golden candlestick was a lamp; these were lighted every evening, and extinguished every morning. They were intended to give light by night. <div eID="gen53412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53413" type="x-p"/> 2. The altar of incense was of gold; and a priest, chosen by lot each week, offered incense every morning and evening in a golden censer, which he probably left on the altar after the completion of the offering. <div eID="gen53413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53414" type="x-p"/> 3. The table of the show-bread was covered with plates of gold; and on this, every Sabbath, they placed twelve loaves in two piles, six in each, which continued there all the week till the next Sabbath, when they were removed, and fresh loaves put in their place. The whole of this may be seen in all its details in the book of Exodus, from chap. 35 to <reference osisRef="Exo.40.1">Exo 40:1</reference>. See Calmet also. <div eID="gen53414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53415" type="x-p"/> Which is called the sanctuary - Ἡτις λεγεται ἁγια· This is called holy. This clause may apply to any of the nouns in this verse, in the nominative case, which are all of the feminine gender; and the adjective ἁγια, holy, may be considered here as the nominative singular feminine, agreeing with ἡτις. Several editions accent the words in reference to this construction. The word σκηνη, tabernacle, may be the proper antecedent; and then we may read ἁγία, instead of ἅγια: but these niceties belong chiefly to grammarians.
entries.d6da0ba89519d88490830b4616c2fe72cde43711: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen53415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53416" type="x-p"/> And after the second veil - The first veil, of which the apostle has not yet spoken, was at the entrance of the holy place, and separated the temple from the court, and prevented the people, and even the Levites, from seeing what was in the holy place. <div eID="gen53416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53417" type="x-p"/> The second veil, of which the apostle speaks here, separated the holy place from the holy of holies. <div eID="gen53417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53418" type="x-p"/> The tabernacle, which is called the Holiest of all - That is, that part of the tabernacle which is called the holy of holies.
entries.ac0d0c436baabeed08f84a8e0d88f8b86e5d56be: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen53418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53419" type="x-p"/> Which had the golden censer - It is evident that the apostle speaks here of the tabernacle built by Moses, and of the state and contents of that tabernacle as they were during the lifetime of Moses. For, as Calmet remarks, in the temple which was afterwards built there were many things added which were not in the tabernacle, and several things left out. The ark of the covenant and the two tables of the law were never found after the return from the Babylonish captivity. We have no proof that, even in the time of Solomon, the golden pot of manna, or the rod of Aaron, was either in or near the ark. In Solomon's temple the holy place was separated from the holy of holies by a solid wall, instead of a veil, and by strong wooden doors, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.6.31-1Kgs.6.33">1Kgs 6:31-33</reference>. In the same temple there was a large vestibule before the holy place; and round about this and the holy of holies there were many chambers in three stories, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.6.5">1Kgs 6:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.6.6">1Kgs 6:6</reference>. But there was nothing of all this in the Mosaic tabernacle; therefore, says Calmet, we need not trouble ourselves to reconcile the various scriptures which mention this subject; some of which refer to the tabernacle, others to Solomon's temple, and others to the temple built by Zorobabel; which places were very different from each other. <div eID="gen53419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53420" type="x-p"/> The apostle says that the golden censer was in the holy of holies; but this is nowhere mentioned by Moses. But he tells us that the high priest went in, once every year, with the golden censer to burn incense; and Calmet thinks this censer was left there all the year, and that its place was supplied by a new one, brought in by the priest the year following. Others think it was left just within the veil, so that the priest, by putting his hand under the curtain, could take it out, and prepare it for his next entrance into the holiest. <div eID="gen53420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53421" type="x-p"/> The ark of the covenant - This was a sort of chest overlaid with plates of gold, in which the two tables of the law, Aaron's rod, the pot of manna, etc., were deposited. Its top, or lid, was the propitiatory or mercy-seat.
entries.4a2ade6d27e0015c1f16a265e9bea6fa1ea49064: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen53421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53422" type="x-p"/> And over it the cherubims of glory - Cherubim is the plural of cherub, and it is absurd to add our plural termination (s) to the plural termination of the Hebrew. The glory here signifies the shechinah or symbol of the Divine presence. <div eID="gen53422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53423" type="x-p"/> Shadowing the mercy-seat - One at each end of the ark, with their faces turned toward each other, but looking down on the cover or propitiatory, ἱλαστηριον, here called the mercy-seat. <div eID="gen53423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53424" type="x-p"/> Of which we cannot now speak particularly - The apostle did not judge any farther account of these to be necessary; and I may be excused from considering them particularly here, having said so much on each in the places where they occur in the Pentateuch. What these point out or signify is thus explained by St. Cyril: Christus licet unus sit, multifariam tamen a nobis intelligitur: Ipse est Tabernaculum propter carnis tegumenturn: Ipse est Mensa, quia noster cibus est et vita: Ipse est Arca habens legem Dei reconditam, quia est Verbum Patris: Ipse est Candelabrum, quia est lux spiritualis: Ipse est Altare incensi, quia est odor suavitatis in sanctificationem: Ipse est Altare holocausti, quia est hostia pro totius mundi vita in cruce oblata. "Although Christ be but one, yet he is understood by us under a variety of forms. He is the Tabernacle, on account of the human body in which he dwelt. He is the Table, because he is our Bread of life. He is the Ark which has the law of God enclosed within, because he is the Word of the Father. He is the Candlestick, because he is our spiritual light. He is the Altar of incense, because he is the sweet-smelling odour of sanctification. He is the Altar of burnt-offering, because he is the victim, by death on the cross, for the sins of the whole world." This father has said, in a few words, what others have employed whole volumes on, by refining, spiritualizing, and allegorizing.
entries.a91545ff55d3fde6bdae33e33fa2d3e38bb6bdef: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen53424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53425" type="x-p"/> When these thing were thus ordained - When the tabernacle was made, and its furniture placed in it, according to the Divine direction. <div eID="gen53425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53426" type="x-p"/> The priests went always into the first Tabernacle - That is, into the first part of the tabernacle, or holy place, into which he went every day twice, accomplishing the services, τας λατρειας επιτελουντες, which included his burning the incense at the morning and evening sacrifice, dressing the lamps, removing the old show-bread and laying on the new, and sprinkling the blood of the sin-offerings before the veil <reference osisRef="Lev.4.6">Lev 4:6</reference> : and for these works he must have constant access to the place.
entries.ab87acff18e4926ab1f1af90134ea4a4d176ab19: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen53426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53427" type="x-p"/> But into the second - That is, the holy of holies, or second part of the tabernacle, the high priest alone, once every year, that is, on one day in the year only, which was the day on which the general atonement was made. The high priest could enter into this place only on one day in the year; but on that day he might enter several times. See Lev. 16. <div eID="gen53427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53428" type="x-p"/> Not without blood - The day prescribed by the law for this great solemnity was the tenth of the month Tisri, in which the high priest brought in the incense or perfumes, which he placed on the golden censer; he brought also the blood of the bullock; and sprinkled some portion of it seven times before the ark, and the veil which separated the holy place from the holy of holies. See <reference osisRef="Lev.16.14">Lev 16:14</reference>. He then came out, and, taking some of the blood of the goat which had been sacrificed, he sprinkled it between the veil and the ark of the covenant, <reference osisRef="Lev.16.15">Lev 16:15</reference>. <div eID="gen53428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53429" type="x-p"/> Which he offered for himself, and for the errors of the people - Ὑπερ των του λαου αγνοηματων· For transgressions of which they were not conscious: there were so many niceties in the ritual worship of the Jews, and so many ways in which they might offend against the law and incur guilt, that it was found necessary to institute sacrifices to atone for these sins of ignorance. And as the high priest was also clothed with infirmity, he required to have an interest in the same sacrifice, on the same account. This was a national sacrifice; and by it the people understood that they were absolved from all the errors of the past year, and that they now had a renewed right of access to the mercy-seat.
entries.66d1869df9e5aebe469204a498c9f0bd9bfda251: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen53429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53430" type="x-p"/> The Holy Ghost this signifying - These services were divinely appointed, and by each of them the Holy Spirit of God is supposed to speak. <div eID="gen53430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53431" type="x-p"/> The way into the holiest - That full access to God was not the common privilege of the people, while the Mosaic economy subsisted. That the apostle means that it is only by Christ that any man and every man can approach God, is evident from <reference osisRef="Heb.10.19-Heb.10.22">Heb 10:19-22</reference>, and it is about this, and not about the tabernacle of this world, that he is here discoursing. <div eID="gen53431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53432" type="x-p"/> I have already observed that the apostle appears to use the word σκηνη, or tabernacle, in the general sense of a dwelling place; and therefore applies it to the temple, which was reputed the house or dwelling place of God, as well as the ancient tabernacle. Therefore, what he speaks here concerning the first tabernacle, may be understood as applying with propriety to the then Jewish temple, as well as to the ancient tabernacle, which, even with all their sacrifices and ceremonies, could not make the way of holiness plain, nor the way to God's favor possible.
entries.8abc72659bc99003dd9ce0c32c3c4a2287ca3a74: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen53432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53433" type="x-p"/> Which - Tabernacle and its services, was a figure, παραβολη, a dark enigmatical representation, for the time then present - for that age and dispensation, and for all those who lived under it. <div eID="gen53433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53434" type="x-p"/> In which, καθ' ὁν, during which, time or dispensation were offered both gifts and sacrifices - eucharistic offerings and victims for sin, that could not make him that did the service, whether the priest who made the offering, or the person who brought it in the behalf of his soul, perfect as pertaining to the conscience - could not take away guilt from the mind, nor purify the conscience from dead works. The whole was a figure, or dark representation, of a spiritual and more glorious system: and although a sinner, who made these offerings and sacrifices according to the law, might be considered as having done his duty, and thus he would be exempted from many ecclesiastical and legal disabilities and punishments; yet his conscience would ever tell him that the guilt of sin was still remaining, and that it was impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take it away. Thus even he that did the service best continued to be imperfect - had a guilty conscience, and an unholy heart. <div eID="gen53434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53435" type="x-p"/> The words καθ' ὁν, in which, referred in the above paraphrase to τον καιρον, the time, are read καθ' ἡν by ABD, and several others, one copy of the Slavonic, the Vulgate, and some of the fathers, and thus refer to την σκηνην, the tabernacle; and this is the reading which our translators appear to have followed. Griesbach places it in his margin, as a very probable reading; but I prefer the other.
entries.073ebd280c5682339cab427d66a674f875d71199: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen53435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53436" type="x-p"/> In meats and drinks, and divers washings - He had already mentioned eucharistic and sacrificial offerings, and nothing properly remained but the different kinds of clean and unclean animals which were used, or forbidden to be used, as articles of food; together with the different kinds or drinks, washings, βαπτισμοις, baptisms, immersions, sprinklings and washings of the body and the clothes, and carnal ordinances, or things which had respect merely to the body, and could have no moral influence upon the soul, unless considered in reference to that of which they were the similitudes, or figures. <div eID="gen53436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53437" type="x-p"/> Carnal ordinances - Δικαιωματα σαρκος· Rites and ceremonies pertaining merely to the body. The word carnal is not used here, nor scarcely in any part of the New Testament, in that catachrestical or degrading sense in which many preachers and professors of Christianity take the liberty to use it. <div eID="gen53437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53438" type="x-p"/> Imposed on them until the time of reformation - These rites and ceremonies were enacted, by Divine authority, as proper representations of the Gospel system, which should reform and rectify all things. <div eID="gen53438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53439" type="x-p"/> The time of reformation, καιρος διορθωσεως, the time of rectifying, signifies the Gospel dispensation, under which every thing is set straight; every thing referred to its proper purpose and end; the ceremonial law fulfilled and abrogated; the moral law exhibited and more strictly enjoined; (see our Lord's sermon upon the mount); and the spiritual nature of God's worship taught, and grace promised to purify the heart: so that, through the power of the eternal Spirit, all that was wrong in the soul is rectified; the affections, passions, and appetites purified; the understanding enlightened; the judgment corrected; the will refined; in a word, all things made new.
entries.f7e220ec7377003f5feeea3d2f04a3c08d6f0926: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen53439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53440" type="x-p"/> But Christ being come a high priest of good things - I think this and the succeeding verses not happily translated: indeed, the division of them has led to a wrong translation; therefore they must be taken together, thus: But the Christ, the high priest of those good things (or services) which were to come, through a greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands, that is, not of the same workmanship, entered once for all into the sanctuary; having obtained eternal redemption for us, not by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.13">Heb 9:13</reference>. For if the blood of Goats, and bulls, and calves, and a heifer's ashes, sprinkled on the unclean, sanctifieth to the cleansing of the flesh, (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.14">Heb 9:14</reference>), how much more shall the blood of Christ, who, through the eternal Spirit, offered himself without spot to God, cleanse your consciences from dead works, in order to worship (or that ye may worship) the living God? <div eID="gen53440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53441" type="x-p"/> In the above translation I have added, in <reference osisRef="Heb.9.13">Heb 9:13</reference>, τραγων, of goats, on the authority of ABDE, three others, the Syriac, the Arabic of Erpen, Coptic, Vulgate, two copies of the Itala, and Theodoret. And I have rendered εις το λατρευειν, (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.14">Heb 9:14</reference>), In Order to worship, or That Ye May worship; for this is the meaning of these particles εις το in many parts of the New Testament. I shall now make a few observations on some of the principal expressions. <div eID="gen53441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53442" type="x-p"/> High priest of good things - Or services, to come, των μελλοντων αγαθων. He is the High Priest of Christianity; he officiates in the behalf of all mankind; for by him are all the prayers, praises, and services of mankind offered to God; and he ever appears in the presence of God for us. <div eID="gen53442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53443" type="x-p"/> A greater and more perfect tabernacle - This appears to mean our Lord's human nature. That, in which dwelt all the fullness of the Godhead bodily, was fitly typified by the tabernacle and temple, in both of which the majesty of God dwelt. <div eID="gen53443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53444" type="x-p"/> Not made with hands - Though our Lord's body was a perfect human body, yet it did not come in the way of natural generation; his miraculous conception will sufficiently justify the expressions used here by the apostle.
entries.5e679d4c5839c7bdee234b7f88a2a635efac5321: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen53444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53445" type="x-p"/> But by his own blood - Here the redemption of man is attributed to the blood of Christ; and this blood is stated to be shed in a sacrificial way, precisely as the blood of bulls, goats and calves was shed under the law. <div eID="gen53445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53446" type="x-p"/> Once - Once for all, εφαπαξ, in opposition to the annual entering of the high priest into the holiest, with the blood of the annual victim. <div eID="gen53446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53447" type="x-p"/> The holy place - Or sanctuary, τα ἁγιᾳ, signifies heaven, into which Jesus entered with his own blood, as the high priest entered into the holy of holies with the blood of the victims which he had sacrificed. <div eID="gen53447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53448" type="x-p"/> Eternal redemption - Αιωνιαν λυτρωσιν· A redemption price which should stand good for ever, when once offered; and an endless redemption from sin, in reference to the pardon of which, and reconciliation to God, there needs no other sacrifice: it is eternal in its merit and efficacy.
entries.ad7582fba310591c7ee303a523b401f441496cfc: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen53448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53449" type="x-p"/> Sanctifieth to the purifying of the flesh - Answers the end proposed by the law; namely, to remove legal disabilities and punishments, having the body and its interests particularly in view, though adumbrating or typifying the soul and its concerns.
entries.3cd2706c4f7b01aaf7f26e8a9507b075d10c0f74: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen53449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53450" type="x-p"/> Who through the eternal Spirit - This expression is understood two ways: <div eID="gen53450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53451" type="x-p"/> 1. Of the Holy Ghost himself. As Christ's miraculous conception was by the Holy Spirit, and he wrought all his miracles by the Spirit of God, so his death or final offering was made through or by the eternal Spirit; and by that Spirit he was raised from the dead, <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.18">1Pet 3:18</reference>. Indeed, through the whole of his life be was justified by the Spirit; and we find that in this great work of human redemption, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit were continually employed: therefore the words may be understood of the Holy Spirit properly. <div eID="gen53451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53452" type="x-p"/> 2. Of the eternal Logos or Deity which dwelt in the man Christ Jesus, through the energy of which the offering of his humanity became an infinitely meritorious victim; therefore the Deity of Christ is here intended. <div eID="gen53452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53453" type="x-p"/> But we cannot well consider one of these distinct from the other; and hence probably arose the various readings in the MSS. and versions on this article. Instead of δια Πνευματος αιωνιου, by the Eternal Spirit, δια Πνευματος Ἁγιου, by the Holy Spirit, is the reading of D*, and more than twenty others of good note, besides the Coptic, Slavonic, Vulgate, two copies of the Itala, Cyril, Athanasius sometimes, Damascenus, Chrysostom, and some others. But the common reading is supported by ABD**, and others, besides the Syriac, all the Arabic, Armenian, Ethiopic, Athanasius generally, Theodoret, Theophylact, and Ambrosius. This, therefore, is the reading that should he preferred, as it is probable that the Holy Ghost, not the Logos, is what the apostle had more immediately in view. But still we must say, that the Holy Spirit, with the eternal Logos, and the almighty Father, equally concurred in offering up the sacrifice of the human nature of Christ, in order to make atonement for the sin of the world. <div eID="gen53453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53454" type="x-p"/> Purge your conscience - Καθαριει την συνειδησιν· Purify your conscience. The term purify should be everywhere, both in the translation of the Scriptures, and in preaching the Gospel, preferred to the word purge, which, at present, is scarcely ever used in the sense in which our translators have employed it. <div eID="gen53454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53455" type="x-p"/> Dead works - Sin in general, or acts to which the penalty of death is annexed by the law. See the phrase explained, <reference osisRef="Heb.6.1">Heb 6:1</reference> (note).
entries.d3dacf47d85304b8a210baf52e07a2dd53442393: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen53455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53456" type="x-p"/> And for this cause - Some translate δια τουτο, on account of this (blood.) Perhaps it means no more than a mere inference, such as therefore, or wherefore. <div eID="gen53456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53457" type="x-p"/> He is the Mediator of the new testament - There was no proper reason why our translators should render διαθηκη by testament here, when in almost every other case they render it covenant, which is its proper ecclesiastical meaning, as answering to the Hebrew ברית berith, which see largely explained, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.10">Gen 15:10</reference>, and in other places of the Pentateuch. <div eID="gen53457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53458" type="x-p"/> Very few persons are satisfied with the translation of the following verses to the 20th, particularly the 16th and 17th; at all events the word covenant must be retained. He - Jesus Christ, is Mediator; the μεσιτης, or mediator, was the person who witnessed the contract made between the two contracting parties, slew the victim, and sprinkled each with its blood. <div eID="gen53458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53459" type="x-p"/> Of the new testament - The new contract betwixt God and the whole human race, by Christ Jesus the Mediator, distinguished here from the old covenant between God and the Israelites, in which Moses was the mediator. <div eID="gen53459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53460" type="x-p"/> That by means of death - His own death upon the cross. <div eID="gen53460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53461" type="x-p"/> For the redemption of the transgressions - To make atonement for the transgressions which were committed under the old covenant, which the blood of bulls and calves could not do; so the death of Jesus had respect to all the time antecedent to it, as well as to all the time afterward till the conclusion of the world. <div eID="gen53461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53462" type="x-p"/> They which are called - The Gentiles, might receive the promise - might, by being brought into a covenant with God, have an equal right with the Jews, not merely to an inheritance such as the promised land, but to an eternal inheritance, and consequently infinitely superior to that of the Jews, inasmuch as the new covenant is superior in every point of view to the old. <div eID="gen53462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53463" type="x-p"/> How frequently the Gentiles are termed οἱ κλητοι and οἱ κεκλημενοι, the called, all St. Paul's writings show. And they were thus termed because they were called and elected in the place of the Jews, the ancient called and elect, who were now divorced and reprobated because of their disobedience.
entries.6cb59cf010061f65d161416e91e35f30dacf8231: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen53463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53464" type="x-p"/> For where a testament is - A learned and judicious friend furnishes me with the following translation of this and the 17th verse: - "For where there is a covenant, it is necessary that the death of the appointed victim should be exhibited, because a covenant is confirmed over dead victims, since it is not at all valid while the appointed victim is alive." <div eID="gen53464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53465" type="x-p"/> He observes, "There is no word signifying testator, or men, in the original. Διαθεμενος is not a substantive, but a participle, or a participial adjective, derived from the same root as διατηκη, and must have a substantive understood. I therefore render it the disposed or appointed victim, alluding to the manner of disposing or setting apart the pieces of the victim, when they were going to ratify a covenant; and you know well the old custom of ratifying a covenant, to which the apostle alludes. I refer to your own notes on <reference osisRef="Gen.6.18">Gen 6:18</reference> (note), and <reference osisRef="Gen.15.10">Gen 15:10</reference> (note). - J. C." <div eID="gen53465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53466" type="x-p"/> Mr. Wakefield has translated the passage nearly in the same way. "For where a covenant is, there must be necessarily introduced the death of that which establisheth the covenant; because a covenant is confirmed over dead things, and is of no force at all whilst that which establisheth the covenant is alive." This is undoubtedly the meaning of this passage; and we should endeavor to forget that testament and testator were ever introduced, as they totally change the apostle's meaning. See the observations at the end of this chapter.
entries.64daa24d14035f95a5284d115ac1c5200a497d2e: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen53466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53467" type="x-p"/> Whereupon - Ὁθεν. Wherefore, as a victim was required for the ratification of every covenant, the first covenant made between God and the Hebrews, by the mediation of Moses, was not dedicated, εγκεκαινισται, renewed or solemnized, without blood - without the death of a victim, and the aspersion of its blood.
entries.cf4d1c8f6ecd0fd2b0e98a6c3a09f18877c4cb61: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen53467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53468" type="x-p"/> When Moses had spoken every precept - The place to which the apostle alludes is <reference osisRef="Exo.24.4-Exo.24.8">Exo 24:4-8</reference>, where the reader is requested to consult the notes. <div eID="gen53468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53469" type="x-p"/> And sprinkled both the book - The sprinkling of the book is not mentioned in the place to which the apostle refers, (see above), nor did it in fact take place. The words αυτο τε το βιβλιον, and the book itself, should be referred to λαβων, having taken, and not to ερῥαντισε, he sprinkled; the verse should therefore be read thus: For after every commandment of the law had been recited by Moses to all the people, he took the blood of the calves, and of the goats, with water and scarlet wool, and the book itself, and sprinkled all the people. The rite was performed thus: Having received the blood of the calves and goats into basins, and mingled it with water to prevent it from coagulating, he then took a bunch of hyssop, and having bound it together with thread made of scarlet wool, he dipped this in the basin, and sprinkled the blood and water upon the people who were nearest to him, and who might be considered on this occasion the representatives of all the rest; for it is impossible that he should have had blood enough to have sprinkled the whole of the congregation. <div eID="gen53469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53470" type="x-p"/> Some think that the blood was actually sprinkled upon the book itself, which contained the written covenant, to signify that the covenant itself was ratified by the blood.
entries.ad080e8dd0d82a68c2f150edcb08ba50008d5673: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen53470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53471" type="x-p"/> This is the blood of the testament - (covenant.) Our Lord refers to the conduct of Moses here, and partly quotes his words in the institution of the eucharist: This is my blood of the new covenant, which is shed for many for the remission of sins, <reference osisRef="Mat.26.28">Mat 26:28</reference>. And by thus using the words and applying them, he shows that his sacrificial blood was intended by the blood shed and sprinkled on this occasion, and that by it alone the remission of sins is obtained.
entries.03a1738086ff2e6bf280ae73229b02825ca44502: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen53471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53472" type="x-p"/> He sprinkled - with blood - all the vessels of the ministry - To intimate that every thing used by sinful man is polluted, and that nothing can be acceptable in the sight of a holy God that has not in effect the sprinkling of the atoning blood.
entries.4fe9b2aa34ae2d0a7bb6dd87a2f9c393fd2aa07b: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen53472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53473" type="x-p"/> And almost all things are - purged with blood - The apostle says almost, because in some cases certain vessels were purified by water, some by fire, <reference osisRef="Num.31.23">Num 31:23</reference>, and some with the ashes of the red heifer, <reference osisRef="Num.19.2-Num.19.10">Num 19:2-10</reference>, but it was always understood that every thing was at first consecrated by the blood of the victim. <div eID="gen53473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53474" type="x-p"/> And without shedding of blood is no remission - The apostle shows fully here what is one of his great objects in the whole of this epistle, viz. that there is no salvation but through the sacrificial death of Christ, and to prefigure this the law itself would not grant any remission of sin without the blood of a victim. This is a maxim even among the Jews themselves, אין כפרה אלא בדם ein capparah ella bedam, "There is no expiation but by blood." Yoma, fol. 5, 1; Menachoth, fol. 93, 2. Every sinner has forfeited his life by his transgressions, and the law of God requires his death; the blood of the victim, which is its life, is shed as a substitute for the life of the sinner. By these victims the sacrifice of Christ was typified. He gave his life for the life of the world; human life for human life, but a life infinitely dignified by its union with God.
entries.f7a0becebfd7c2c6b25b26694e12fb2693e953f2: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen53474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53475" type="x-p"/> The patterns of things in the heavens - That is: The tabernacle and all its utensils, services, etc., must be purified by these, viz.: The blood of calves and goats, and the sprinkling of the blood and water with the bunch of hyssop bound about with scarlet wool. These are called patterns, ὑποδειγματα, exemplars, earthly things, which were the representatives of heavenly things. And there is no doubt that every thing in the tabernacle, its parts, divisions, utensils, ministry, etc., as appointed by God, were representations of celestial matters; but how far and in what way we cannot now see. <div eID="gen53475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53476" type="x-p"/> Purification implies, not only cleansing from defilement, but also dedication or consecration. All the utensils employed in the tabernacle service were thus purified though incapable of any moral pollution. <div eID="gen53476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53477" type="x-p"/> But the heavenly things themselves - <div eID="gen53477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53478" type="x-p"/> 1. Some think this means heaven itself, which, by receiving the sacrificed body of Christ, which appears in the presence of God for us, may be said to be purified, i.e., set apart for the reception of the souls of those who have found redemption in his blood. <div eID="gen53478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53479" type="x-p"/> 2. Others think the body of Christ is intended, which is the tabernacle in which his Divinity dwelt; and that this might be said to be purified by its own sacrifice, as he is said, <reference osisRef="Joh.17.19">Joh 17:19</reference>, to sanctify himself; that is, to consecrate himself unto God as a sin-offering for the redemption of man. <div eID="gen53479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53480" type="x-p"/> 3. Others suppose the Church is intended, which he is to present to the Father without spot or wrinkle or any such thing. <div eID="gen53480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53481" type="x-p"/> 4. As the entrance to the holy of holies must be made by the sprinkling of the blood of the sacrifice, and as that holy of holies represented heaven, the apostle's meaning seems to be that there was and could be no entrance to the holiest but through his blood; and therefore, when by a more perfect tabernacle, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.11">Heb 9:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.12">Heb 9:12</reference>, he passed into the heavens, not with the blood of bulls and goats, but by his own blood, he thus purified or laid open the entrance to the holiest, by a more valuable sacrifice than those required to open the entrance of the holy of holies. It was necessary, therefore, for God had appointed it so, that the tabernacle and its parts, etc., which were patterns of things in the heavens, should be consecrated and entered with such sacrifices as have already been mentioned; but the heaven of heavens into which Jesus entered, and whither he will bring all his faithful followers, must be propitiated, consecrated, and entered, by the infinitely better sacrifice of his own body and blood. That this is the meaning appears from the following verse.
entries.bd454e03843a13568563f36bae85a5bb48796c6c: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen53481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53482" type="x-p"/> Christ is not entered into the holy places made with hands - He is not gone into the holy of holies of the tabernacle or temple, as the Jewish high priest does once in the year with the blood of the victim, to sprinkle it before the mercy-seat there; but into heaven itself, which he has thus opened to all believers, having made the propitiatory offering by which both he and those whom he represents are entitled to enter and enjoy eternal blessedness. And hence we may consider that Christ, appearing in his crucified body before the throne, is a real offering of himself to the Divine justice in behalf of man; and that there he continues in the constant act of being offered, so that every penitent and believer, coming unto God through him, find him their ever ready and available sacrifice, officiating as the High Priest of mankind in the presence of God.
entries.77f88904cdb3f1d03d7a9992751c8fa8c879cfca: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen53482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53483" type="x-p"/> Nor yet that he should offer himself often - The sacrifice of Christ is not like that of the Jewish high priest; his must be offered every year, Christ has offered himself once for all: and this sacrificial act has ever the same efficacy, his crucified body being still a powerful and infinitely meritorious sacrifice before the throne.
entries.29fb9a41fa8409f213225ceeb10782d20b691258: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen53483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53484" type="x-p"/> For then must he often have suffered - In the counsel of God, Christ was considered the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world, <reference osisRef="Rev.13.8">Rev 13:8</reference>, so that all believers before his advent were equally interested in his sacrificial death with those who have lived since his coming. Humanly speaking, the virtue of the annual atonement could not last long, and must be repeated; Christ's sacrifice is ever the same; his life's blood is still considered as in the act of being continually poured out. See <reference osisRef="Rev.5.6">Rev 5:6</reference>. <div eID="gen53484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53485" type="x-p"/> The end of the world - The conclusion of the Jewish dispensation, the Christian dispensation being that which shall continue till the end of time. <div eID="gen53485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53486" type="x-p"/> To put away sin - Εις αθετησιν ἁμαρτιας· To abolish the sin-offerings; i.e. to put an end to the Mosaic economy by his one offering of himself. It is certain that, after Christ had offered himself, the typical sin-offerings of the law ceased; and this was expressly foretold by the Prophet Daniel, <reference osisRef="Dan.9.24">Dan 9:24</reference>. Some think that the expression should be applied to the putting away the guilt, power, and being of sin from the souls of believers.
entries.90b8b77491bd0e52862398a89ade9fbeb7e7a407: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen53486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53487" type="x-p"/> As it is appointed - Αποκειται· It is laid before them by the Divine decree: Dust thou art, and unto dust thou shalt return.
